interviewQuestions.question: How would you assign a delivery partner when both restaurant prep time and partner availability are unpredictable?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd frame the two failure modes first: assign too early and the partner idles at the restaurant; assign too late and the delivery is slower than it needs to be because search-and-travel time stacks on top of prep time.

My approach is to predict restaurant-ready-time — from that restaurant's historical prep times, or a live signal the restaurant provides — and time partner search so the partner's estimated arrival lines up with food actually being ready. For restaurants with volatile prep times, I'd bias toward assigning later and accept slightly higher delivery latency over partner idle time, since idle partners hurt the whole marketplace, not just one order.

I'd close by noting this needs a feedback loop — comparing predicted vs actual ready-time per restaurant to keep the prediction honest over time.

**Testing:** whether you can reason about a two-sided timing problem instead of picking one fixed assignment-time rule.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Timing delivery-partner assignment

interviewQuestions.question: How would refunds and partial refunds change the order state machine?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd point out that a full refund maps cleanly onto the existing CANCELLED state — the order never completes, money comes back. A partial refund is trickier because the order still completes (food was delivered) but one line item wasn't fulfilled as ordered, so it can't reuse CANCELLED without lying about what actually happened.

I'd add a distinct terminal state, something like DELIVERED_WITH_ADJUSTMENT, reachable from the partial-fulfillment event I'd already modeled (an item going out of stock mid-prep), and I'd keep a record of exactly which lines were refunded and why, since that's needed for both customer support and restaurant payout reconciliation.

I'd close by noting refunds shouldn't be a side effect bolted onto the Order class — a PaymentService should own the actual refund call and report back a status the order records.

**Testing:** whether you extend a state machine cleanly for a new real-world case instead of overloading an existing state.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Refunds and the order state machine

interviewQuestions.question: Why does Order need its own explicit state machine instead of a free-text status string that whichever service touches it last just overwrites?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start with the concrete failure a free-text field invites: nothing stops a delivery-partner service from writing "DELIVERED" onto an order the restaurant service never marked as prepared, or two services racing to write different strings within the same second with no rule for which wins. A string has no memory of what transitions are even legal.

With an explicit state machine — PLACED, CONFIRMED, PREPARING, READY_FOR_PICKUP, OUT_FOR_DELIVERY, DELIVERED, CANCELLED — each transition is validated against the order's *current* state before it's applied, so a delivery partner can't mark DELIVERED on an order that's still PREPARING, and the transition itself is the single place side effects live: moving to OUT_FOR_DELIVERY is what triggers the customer notification, not a side comment appended somewhere else.

The three actors — restaurant, delivery partner, customer app — each only get to trigger the transitions that are theirs to trigger (the restaurant can't mark OUT_FOR_DELIVERY; the partner can't mark CONFIRMED), which is easy to enforce against a real state machine and nearly impossible to enforce against a free-text field with no defined vocabulary.

**Testing:** whether you recognize that a shared mutable field written by multiple independent services needs an enforced contract, not just an agreed-upon convention.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why Order needs an explicit state machine

interviewQuestions.question: Two orders from the same restaurant become ready within seconds of each other and only one nearby delivery partner is available — how do you decide who gets assigned first?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd reject pure FIFO-by-ready-time as the whole answer, since it ignores information the system already has: which order the partner can complete faster given both orders' delivery distances, and how long each customer has already waited relative to their promised ETA. A naive first-ready-first-assigned rule can strand a customer who ordered earlier but got unlucky with restaurant prep time.

I'd model the assignment decision as a small scoring function evaluated across the contested partner and both candidate orders — factoring in each order's elapsed wait time (customers who've waited longer get priority weight), the incremental detour cost of taking one order over the other given the partner's current location, and any SLA risk (an order about to breach its promised delivery window gets a strong boost). The partner goes to whichever order scores higher, and the loser re-enters the assignment queue and searches for the next-nearest available partner rather than waiting for this one.

I'd flag the trade-off explicitly: this is more computation than "whoever's ready first wins," and for a system with many available partners this contention is rare enough that the simple rule is fine — the scoring approach earns its complexity specifically under partner scarcity.

**Testing:** whether you can design a tie-breaking rule using real signals (wait time, detour cost, SLA risk) instead of an arbitrary default, and know when the added complexity is actually warranted.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Contention for a scarce delivery partner
